nodes.name: Height of a frieze pattern
nodes.statement: For us, the height of a frieze pattern corresponds to the number of rows, including the rows of ones but {\it excluding} the rows of zeros.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Height counts the rows of a frieze pattern including the rows of ones, excluding the rows of zeros.

nodes.name: Fixed field F
nodes.statement: Throughout this section, we fix an arbitrary field $F$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns

nodes.name: F-valued pattern of height n
nodes.statement: Fix $n \in \mathbb{N}^*$. A map $f : \{0,1,\ldots , n,n+1\} \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow F$ is called an \textit{$F$-valued pattern of height n} if, 1) for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, $ f(0,m) = f (n+1,m) = 0$, 2) for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, $ f(1,m) = f (n,m) = 1$, and 3) for all $(i,m) \in \{1,2,\ldots , n\} \times \mathbb{Z}$, we have \begin{equation} f(i,m) f(i,m+1) = 1 + f(i+1,m) f(i-1, m+1). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: A map on rows 0..n+1 by Z with zero boundary rows, rows of ones, and the unimodular diamond rule.
nodes.label: def:pattern_n

nodes.name: Diamond rule
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Unimodular diamond rule for frieze patterns.
nodes.label: eq:diamond

nodes.name: Nowhere-zero pattern
nodes.statement: An $F$-valued pattern $f$ of height $n$ is said to be {\it nowhere zero} if $f(i,m) \neq 0$, for all $i \in \{1,\ldots , n\}$ and for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
differentia: $f(i,m) \neq 0$, for all $i \in \{1,\ldots , n\}$ and for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$

nodes.name: Continuant recurrence for patterns
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$. For all $m$, we have \begin{align*} f(i+2,m) &= f(2,m+i) f(i+1,m) - f(i,m), \qquad i \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\} \\ f (i,m) &= f (n-1,m) f (i+1,m-1) - f(i+2,m-2), \qquad i \in \{0,n-1\}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
assumptions: Let $f$ be a nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$.
nodes.statement_short: In a nowhere-zero pattern, columns satisfy three-term linear recurrences with coefficients from rows 2 and n-1.
nodes.label: l:pattern_nContinuant

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: We begin by proving the first statement. That is, we prove \[ P_i : \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, f(i+2,m) = f(2,m+i+1) f(i+1,m) - f(i,m), \] for $ i \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$. We do so by induction on $i$. Base case $P_0$: We have that for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, $f(2,m) f(1,m) - f(0,m) = f (2,m+1)*1 - 0 = f (2,m)$. Inductive hypothesis. Suppose that our claim holds for some $i \in \{0,\ldots, n-2\}$ fixed. Then, \begin{align*} f (i+3,m) f (i+1,m+1) & = f (i+2,m) f (i+2,m+1)-1 \\ &= f (i+2,m) (f(2,m+i+1) f(i+1,m+1) - f(i,m+1)) -1 \\ &= f (i+2,m) f (2,m+i+1) f (i+1,m+1) - (f (i+2,m)f (i,m+1) + 1) \\ &= f (i+2,m) f (2,m+i+1) f (i+1,m+1) - f(i+1,m) f (i+1,m+1). \end{align*} Since $f$ is nowhere-zero, we may divide both sides of the equation by $f (i+1,m+1)$ to obtain the desired equality. The second statement is proved almost identically. Namely, we prove \[ Q_i: \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, f (i,m) = f (n-1,m) f (i+1,m-1) - f(i+2,m-2), \] by induction on $i$, starting with $i = n-1$ and proving the inductive step $Q_i \Rightarrow Q_{i-1}$. Base case $Q_{n-1}$: for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, $ f (n-1,m) f (n,m-1) - f(n+1,m-2) = f (n-1,m)*1 - 0 = f (n-1,m)$. Inductive hypothesis. Suppose that $Q_{i+1}$ holds for some fixed $i \in \{0,\ldots, n-2\}$. Then, \begin{align*} f (i,m) f (i+2,m-1) &= f (i+1,m-1) f (i+1,m) - 1\\ &= f (i+1,m-1) (f (i+2,m-1) f (n-1,m) - f(i+3,m-2)) -1 \\ &= f (i+1,m-1)f (n-1,m) f (i+2,m-1) - (f (i+1,m-1) f (i+3,m-2) + 1) \\ &= f (i+1,m-1)f (n-1,m) f (i+2,m-1) - f (i+2,m-2) f (i+2,m-1). \end{align*} Again since $f$ is nowhere-zero, dividing by $f (i+2,m-1)$ on both sides we obtain $Q_i$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Two inductions on $i$, using the diamond rule and dividing by nonzero entries.

nodes.name: Set up induction for first identity
nodes.statement: We begin by proving the first statement. That is, we prove \[ P_i : \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, f(i+2,m) = f(2,m+i+1) f(i+1,m) - f(i,m), \] for $ i \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$. We do so by induction on $i$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: State $P_i$ and set up induction on $i$.

nodes.name: Base case P_0
nodes.statement: Base case $P_0$: We have that for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, $f(2,m) f(1,m) - f(0,m) = f (2,m+1)*1 - 0 = f (2,m)$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Verify base case $P_0$ from boundary rows.

nodes.name: Inductive step for P_i
nodes.statement: Inductive hypothesis. Suppose that our claim holds for some $i \in \{0,\ldots, n-2\}$ fixed. Then, \begin{align*} f (i+3,m) f (i+1,m+1) & = f (i+2,m) f (i+2,m+1)-1 \\ &= f (i+2,m) (f(2,m+i+1) f(i+1,m+1) - f(i,m+1)) -1 \\ &= f (i+2,m) f (2,m+i+1) f (i+1,m+1) - (f (i+2,m)f (i,m+1) + 1) \\ &= f (i+2,m) f (2,m+i+1) f (i+1,m+1) - f(i+1,m) f (i+1,m+1). \end{align*} Since $f$ is nowhere-zero, we may divide both sides of the equation by $f (i+1,m+1)$ to obtain the desired equality.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Expand with diamond rule and hypothesis, divide by nonzero entry.

nodes.name: Set up induction for second identity
nodes.statement: The second statement is proved almost identically. Namely, we prove \[ Q_i: \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, f (i,m) = f (n-1,m) f (i+1,m-1) - f(i+2,m-2), \] by induction on $i$, starting with $i = n-1$ and proving the inductive step $Q_i \Rightarrow Q_{i-1}$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: State $Q_i$ and set up downward induction.

nodes.name: Base case Q_{n-1}
nodes.statement: Base case $Q_{n-1}$: for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, $ f (n-1,m) f (n,m-1) - f(n+1,m-2) = f (n-1,m)*1 - 0 = f (n-1,m)$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Verify base case $Q_{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Inductive step for Q_i
nodes.statement: Inductive hypothesis. Suppose that $Q_{i+1}$ holds for some fixed $i \in \{0,\ldots, n-2\}$. Then, \begin{align*} f (i,m) f (i+2,m-1) &= f (i+1,m-1) f (i+1,m) - 1\\ &= f (i+1,m-1) (f (i+2,m-1) f (n-1,m) - f(i+3,m-2)) -1 \\ &= f (i+1,m-1)f (n-1,m) f (i+2,m-1) - (f (i+1,m-1) f (i+3,m-2) + 1) \\ &= f (i+1,m-1)f (n-1,m) f (i+2,m-1) - f (i+2,m-2) f (i+2,m-1). \end{align*} Again since $f$ is nowhere-zero, dividing by $f (i+2,m-1)$ on both sides we obtain $Q_i$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Expand with diamond rule, divide by nonzero entry to get $Q_i$.

nodes.name: Translation invariance of nowhere-zero patterns
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$. Then, for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and all $i \in \{0,\ldots, n+1\}$, we have \[ f(i,m) = f(i,m+n+1). \]
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
assumptions: Let $f$ be a nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$.
conclusions: for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and all $i \in \{0,\ldots, n+1\}$, we have \[ f(i,m) = f(i,m+n+1). \]
nodes.statement_short: Nowhere-zero patterns of height $n$ are periodic with period $n+1$.
nodes.label: prop:translationInvariance

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1 (glide symmetry)
nodes.statement: We prove a stronger statement, called the \textit{glide symmetry} of frieze patterns. First, consider the map $\rho_n: \{0,1,\ldots , n+1\} \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \{0,1,\ldots , n+1\} \times \mathbb{Z}$ given by \begin{equation} \rho_n(i,m) = (n+1-i, m+i). \end{equation} We show that every nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$ is $\rho_n$-invariant, i.e. satisfies \[ f(\rho_n(i,m)) = f(i,m), \qquad \forall (i,m) \in \{0,1,\ldots , n+1\} \times \mathbb{Z}. \] The proposition will then follow by observing that $\rho_n^2 : (i,m) \mapsto (i,m+n+1)$. Thus, consider the statement \[ P_i: \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, f (i,m) = f (n+1-i,m+i), \] where $i \in \{0, \ldots, n+1\}$. To prove that $P_i$ holds for all $i$, it is sufficient to prove that $P_0, P_1$ hold, and that $P_i \wedge P_{i+1} \Rightarrow P_{i+2}$. $P_0:$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}, f(0,m) = 0 = f(n+1,m)$. $P_1:$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}, f(1,m) = 1 = f(n,m+1)$. Now suppose we are given $i \in \{0,1,\ldots , n-1\}$ such that $P_i$ and $P_{i+1}$ hold. Then, for any fixed $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, we have \begin{align*} f(i+2,m) &= f(2,m+i) f(i+1,m) - f(i,m)\\ &= f (n-1,m+i+2) f (n-i,m+i+1) - f (n+1- i, m + i) \\ &= f (n-i-1,m + i + 2). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Prove the stronger glide symmetry $f\circ\rho_n = f$ by two-step induction on $i$ using Lemma 1; periodicity follows since $\rho_n^2$ is translation by $n+1$.

nodes.name: Introduce glide map
nodes.statement: We prove a stronger statement, called the \textit{glide symmetry} of frieze patterns. First, consider the map $\rho_n: \{0,1,\ldots , n+1\} \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \{0,1,\ldots , n+1\} \times \mathbb{Z}$ given by \begin{equation} \rho_n(i,m) = (n+1-i, m+i). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the glide map $\rho_n$.

nodes.name: Claim: glide symmetry
nodes.statement: We show that every nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$ is $\rho_n$-invariant, i.e. satisfies \[ f(\rho_n(i,m)) = f(i,m), \qquad \forall (i,m) \in \{0,1,\ldots , n+1\} \times \mathbb{Z}. \] The proposition will then follow by observing that $\rho_n^2 : (i,m) \mapsto (i,m+n+1)$. Thus, consider the statement \[ P_i: \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, f (i,m) = f (n+1-i,m+i), \] where $i \in \{0, \ldots, n+1\}$. To prove that $P_i$ holds for all $i$, it is sufficient to prove that $P_0, P_1$ hold, and that $P_i \wedge P_{i+1} \Rightarrow P_{i+2}$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Claim $\rho_n$-invariance and reduce it to a two-step induction.

nodes.name: Reduce to glide symmetry
nodes.statement: The proposition will then follow by observing that $\rho_n^2 : (i,m) \mapsto (i,m+n+1)$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity follows since $\rho_n^2$ is translation by $n+1$.

nodes.name: Define P_i
nodes.statement: Thus, consider the statement \[ P_i: \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, f (i,m) = f (n+1-i,m+i), \] where $i \in \{0, \ldots, n+1\}$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Define statements $P_i$.

nodes.name: Two-step induction scheme
nodes.statement: To prove that $P_i$ holds for all $i$, it is sufficient to prove that $P_0, P_1$ hold, and that $P_i \wedge P_{i+1} \Rightarrow P_{i+2}$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: $P_0$, $P_1$ and $P_i\wedge P_{i+1}\Rightarrow P_{i+2}$.

nodes.name: Base case P_0
nodes.statement: $P_0:$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}, f(0,m) = 0 = f(n+1,m)$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Base case from zero rows.

nodes.name: Base case P_1
nodes.statement: $P_1:$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}, f(1,m) = 1 = f(n,m+1)$.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Base case from rows of ones.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Now suppose we are given $i \in \{0,1,\ldots , n-1\}$ such that $P_i$ and $P_{i+1}$ hold. Then, for any fixed $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, we have \begin{align*} f(i+2,m) &= f(2,m+i) f(i+1,m) - f(i,m)\\ &= f (n-1,m+i+2) f (n-i,m+i+1) - f (n+1- i, m + i) \\ &= f (n-i-1,m + i + 2). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Apply the continuant recurrence and hypotheses to get $P_{i+2}$.

nodes.name: Glide map
nodes.statement: \rho_n(i,m) = (n+1-i, m+i).
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: Glide reflection $\rho_n(i,m)=(n+1-i,m+i)$.
nodes.label: def:glide

nodes.name: Finiteness of the image
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$. Then, ${\rm Im}(f) := \{f (i,m) : i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}, m \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ is a finite set.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
assumptions: Let $f$ be a nowhere-zero $F$-valued pattern of height $n$.
conclusions: ${\rm Im}(f) := \{f (i,m) : i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}, m \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ is a finite set.
nodes.statement_short: A nowhere-zero pattern takes finitely many values.
nodes.label: cor:imageFinite

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: Consider the finite set $\mathcal{D} = \{(i,m) : i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}, m \in \{0,\ldots, n\}\}$. By Proposition \ref{prop:translationInvariance}, \[ {\rm Im}(f) = \{f (i,m) : (i,m) \in \mathcal{D}\}, \] and the right-hand side is obviously finite.
nodes.section: 1 Field-valued patterns
nodes.statement_short: By periodicity, the image equals the values on a finite fundamental domain.

nodes.name: Pandean sequence and Pan flute
nodes.statement: A sequence $(a_k)$, indexed by $\mathbb{N}^*$ and consisting of positive integers is called pandean if $a_1 = 1$ and if, for every $k > 1$, we have \[ a_k \mid a_{k-1} + a_{k+1}. \] Given a pandean sequence $(a_k)$, if there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $a_k = a_{k+n-1}$ for all $k\in \mathbb{N}$, the tuple $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ is called a Pan flute, or simply a flute, of height $n$. The set of all flutes of a given height $n$ is denoted Flute$(n)$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.genus: A sequence $(a_k)$, indexed by $\mathbb{N}^*$ and consisting of positive integers
differentia: for every $k > 1$, we have \[ a_k \mid a_{k-1} + a_{k+1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Pandean: positive integer sequence with $a_1=1$ and $a_k\mid a_{k-1}+a_{k+1}$; a flute of height $n$ is a periodic block; Flute$(n)$ is the set of them.
nodes.label: def:flute

nodes.name: End entries of a flute are 1
nodes.statement: Note that in a flute of height $n$, the first and last entries are equal to $1$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
conclusions: the first and last entries are equal to $1$

nodes.name: Flute(n) is non-empty
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $n$, the set Flute$(n)$ is non-empty.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.label: l:nFluteNonEmpty

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: It is clear that the constant sequence consisting entirely of ones is pandean, and such a pandean sequence gives rise to a flute of height $n$ for any $n$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement_short: The all-ones sequence is pandean and gives a flute of every height.

nodes.name: Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement: Recall that the Fibonacci sequence $(F_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is defined by $F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1$ and the recursive formula \[ F_k = F_{k-1} + F_{k-2}. \]
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence

nodes.name: Fibonacci flutes
nodes.statement: 1) If $n$ is odd, the $n$-tuple \[ (F_2,F_4, F_6, \ldots, F_{n-1}, F_{n}, F_{n-2}, F_{n-4}, \ldots, F_5, F_3, F_1), \] is a Pan flute of height $n$. 2) If $n$ is even, the $n$-tuple \[ (F_2, F_4, F_6, \ldots, F_{n-2}, F_{n}, F_{n-1}, F_{n-3}, \ldots, F_5, F_3,F_1), \] is a Pan flute of height $n$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
conclusions: the $n$-tuple \[ (F_2,F_4, F_6, \ldots, F_{n-1}, F_{n}, F_{n-2}, F_{n-4}, \ldots, F_5, F_3, F_1), \] is a Pan flute of height $n$.
the $n$-tuple \[ (F_2, F_4, F_6, \ldots, F_{n-2}, F_{n}, F_{n-1}, F_{n-3}, \ldots, F_5, F_3,F_1), \] is a Pan flute of height $n$.
the $n$-tuple \[ (F_2,F_4, F_6, \ldots, F_{n-1}, F_{n}, F_{n-2}, F_{n-4}, \ldots, F_5, F_3, F_1), \] is a Pan flute of height $n$.
the $n$-tuple \[ (F_2, F_4, F_6, \ldots, F_{n-2}, F_{n}, F_{n-1}, F_{n-3}, \ldots, F_5, F_3,F_1), \] is a Pan flute of height $n$.

nodes.statement_short: Interleaving even- and odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers gives a Pan flute of height $n$ containing $F_n$.
nodes.label: l:FibFlute

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: These are a tedious but straightforward calculation.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement_short: Direct calculation (omitted).

nodes.name: Flute reduction lemma
nodes.statement: In a flute $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$, one of the following two statements holds. 1) $a_2 = 1$ or $a_{n-1} =1$. 2) There exists an index $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$ such that $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
conclusions: one of the following two statements holds.
2) There exists an index $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$ such that $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every flute has $a_2=1$, $a_{n-1}=1$, or an entry equal to the sum of its neighbours.
nodes.label: lem:FluteReduction

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Suppose that 1) does not hold. In particular, $a_2 - a_1 > 0$ and $a_n - a_{n-1} < 0$. We prove that statement 2) holds by contradiction. Thus, assume that for all $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$, we have $a_i \neq a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$. Since the $a_i$ are positive integers, we necessarily have $a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} \geq 2 a_i$ for all $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$. Thus, for a given $i$, we have \[ a_{i+1} - a_i = a_{i+1} + a_{i-1} - a_{i-1} - a_i \geq 2 a_i - a_{i-1} - a_i = a_i - a_{i-1}. \] Gathering these inequalities, we obtain \[ a_n - a_{n-1} \geq a_{n-1} - a_{n-2} \geq \ldots \geq a_2 - a_1 > 0, \] which contradicts the fact that $a_n - a_{n-1} < 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: otherwise $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\ge 2a_i$, so successive differences increase, contradicting $a_n-a_{n-1}<0$.

nodes.name: Assume 1) fails
nodes.statement: Suppose that 1) does not hold. In particular, $a_2 - a_1 > 0$ and $a_n - a_{n-1} < 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement_short: Assume 1) fails, so the first difference is positive and the last negative.

nodes.name: Prove 2) by contradiction
nodes.statement: We prove that statement 2) holds by contradiction. Thus, assume that for all $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$, we have $a_i \neq a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$. Since the $a_i$ are positive integers, we necessarily have $a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} \geq 2 a_i$ for all $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$. Thus, for a given $i$, we have \[ a_{i+1} - a_i = a_{i+1} + a_{i-1} - a_{i-1} - a_i \geq 2 a_i - a_{i-1} - a_i = a_i - a_{i-1}. \] Gathering these inequalities, we obtain \[ a_n - a_{n-1} \geq a_{n-1} - a_{n-2} \geq \ldots \geq a_2 - a_1 > 0, \] which contradicts the fact that $a_n - a_{n-1} < 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: differences form a non-decreasing chain.

nodes.name: Assume no sum entry
nodes.statement: Thus, assume that for all $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$, we have $a_i \neq a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement_short: Assume no entry equals the sum of its neighbours.

nodes.name: Divisibility gives convexity
nodes.statement: Since the $a_i$ are positive integers, we necessarily have $a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} \geq 2 a_i$ for all $i \in \{2,\ldots, n-1\}$.
nodes.section: 2 Pandean sequences, flutes and the Fibonacci sequence
nodes.statement_short: Divisibility forces $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\ge 2a_i$.

nodes.name: Differences increase

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Consider the statement \[ P_n: \text{If }(a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in {\rm Flute}(n) \text{, then }a_i \leq F_n \text{ for all }i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}. \] The proposition claims that $P_n$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}^*$. We prove this by induction on $n$. The base case $n = 1$ is clear, since the only flute of height $1$ is $(1)$, and $F_1 = 1$. Similarly, the case $n = 2$ is clear, since the only flute of height $2$ is $(1,1)$, and $F_2 = 1$. Now, assume that $P_k$ holds for all $k$ up to and including a fixed $n \in \mathbb{N}^*$. Let $(a_1, \ldots, a_{n+1}) \in {\rm Flute}(n+1)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:FluteReduction}, we have either $a_2 = 1$ or $a_n = 1$, or there exists an index $i \in \{2,\ldots, n\}$ such that $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$. Suppose that $a_2 = 1$. Then $(a_1, a_3, \ldots, a_{n+1}) \in {\rm Flute}(n)$, and so by the induction hypothesis, $a_i \leq F_n$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$. Since $F_n \leq F_{n+1}$, we have $a_i \leq F_{n+1}$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$. A similar argument applies if $a_n = 1$. Now, suppose that there exists an index $i \in \{2,\ldots, n\}$ such that \begin{equation} a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}. \end{equation} We claim that $(a_1, a_2, \ldots , a_{i-1}, \widehat{a_i}, a_{i+1}, \ldots, a_{n+1}) \in {\rm Flute}(n)$, where $\widehat{a_i}$ means we omit $a_i$. Again by the induction hypothesis, we have that \begin{equation} a_j \leq F_n, \qquad j \neq i. \end{equation} It remains to show that $a_i \leq F_{n+1}$. To see this, note that \eqref{eq:ai} and \eqref{eq:ajs} together imply it is sufficient to show that either $a_{i-1}$ or $a_{i+1}$ is bounded above by $F_{n-1}$. But recall that $a_{i-1}$ and $a_{i+1}$ both belong to the flute $(a_1, a_2, \ldots , a_{i-1}, \widehat{a_i}, a_{i+1}, \ldots, a_{n+1}) $ of height $n$. Thus, the conditions of Lemma \ref{lem:FluteReduction} apply to this flute, so that by a reduction argument identical to the one above, there exists a flute of height $n-1$ containing either $a_{i-1}$ or $a_{i+1}$ (or both !), whereby at least one of the two is bounded above by $F_{n-1}$. This completes the induction step, and the proposition follows.

nodes.name: Arithmetic frieze pattern
nodes.statement: A $\mathbb{Q}$-valued pattern of height $n$ is said to be an \textit{arithmetic frieze pattern} if it takes values in $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$. We denote by Frieze$(n)$ the set of arithmetic frieze patterns of height $n$.

nodes.name: Arithmetic friezes correspond to flutes
nodes.statement: 1) Let $f$ be an arithmetic frieze pattern of height $n$. For all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, the $n$-tuple \[ (f (1,m), f (2,m), \ldots, f (n,m)) \] is a flute of height $n$. 2) Given a flute $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$, there exists a arithmetic frieze pattern $f$ of height $n$ such that \[ (f (1,0), \ldots, f (n,0)) = (a_1, \ldots, a_n). \]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: 1) Note that we have $f(1,0) = f(n,0) = 1$ by definition. Moreover, $f$ is arithmetic and so the first equation in Lemma \ref{l:pattern_nContinuant} is precisely the divisibility condition defining a flute. 2) By arguing recursively, one can construct a pattern $f$ such that $ (f (1,0), \ldots, f (n,0)) = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)$. Moreover, such a frieze pattern is necessarily positive and $\mathbb{Q}$-valued. It remains to show that $f$ is integer-valued. We begin by showing that $f (2,m) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$. By the definition of a flute, $f (2,0) \in \mathbb{Z}$, and for each $i \in \{1,\ldots, n-2\}$, there exists a positive integer $c_i$ such that \[ f(i+1,0) * c_i = f (i+2,0) + f (i,0). \] Using the first equation in Lemma \ref{l:pattern_nContinuant}, we deduce that $f(2,i) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for $i =0, \ldots, n-2$. Moreover, $ f (2,n-1) = f (n-1,0) \in \mathbb{Z}$ by assumption. Thus we have proved that $f (2,m) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for $m = 0, \ldots, n-1$. To see that $f (2,n) \in \mathbb{Z}$, note from Lemma \ref{l:pattern_nContinuant} that $f (2,n) = f (n-1,1)$ can be expressed as a {\it polynomial} with integer coefficients in the variables $f (2,1), f (2,2),\ldots , f (2,n-2)$. The claim for all $m$ then follows from Proposition \ref{prop:translationInvariance}. To see how this implies that $f (i,m) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i \in \{2, \ldots, n\}$, it suffices to see, again from Lemma \ref{l:pattern_nContinuant}, that every $f (i,m)$ can be expressed as a {\it polynomial} with integer coefficients in the variables $f (2,m), f (2,m+1),\ldots , f (2,m+i-2)$.

nodes.name: Maximum value u_n
nodes.statement: By combining Proposition \ref{prop:friezeIffFlute} with Proposition \ref{prop:FluteBounded}, we see that for each $n$, there is a well-defined positive integer, called the {\it maximum value} among arithmetic frieze patterns of height $n$, defined by \[ u_n := \max ( f (i,m) : f \in {\rm Frieze}(n), i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}, m \in \mathbb{Z}). \]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:friezeIffFlute}, every entry of an arithmetic frieze pattern of height $n$ belongs to a flute of height $n$. By Proposition \ref{prop:FluteBounded}, entries in a flute of height $n$ are bounded above by $F_n$. Thus $u_n \leq F_n$ for all $n$. On the other hand, Lemma \ref{l:FibFlute} and 2) of Proposition \ref{prop:friezeIffFlute} show that there exists an arithmetic frieze pattern of height $n$ containing $F_n$ as a value.

nodes.statement_short: Every entry lies in a flute.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:FluteBounded}, entries in a flute of height $n$ are bounded above by $F_n$. Thus $u_n \leq F_n$ for all $n$.
nodes.section: 3 Maximal values of arithmetic frieze patterns
nodes.statement_short: Flute bound gives $u_n\le F_n$.

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: On the other hand, Lemma \ref{l:FibFlute} and 2) of Proposition \ref{prop:friezeIffFlute} show that there exists an arithmetic frieze pattern of height $n$ containing $F_n$ as a value.
nodes.section: 3 Maximal values of arithmetic frieze patterns
nodes.statement_short: Fibonacci flute realizes $F_n$.
